5e1238210ad7192d: OCTOBER 3 — The so-called Blue Wave in Malaysian politics has been stopped. Even if Barisan Nasional (BN) wins Melaka hands down, that would not necessarily revive it.
Indeed, a decisive BN victory could demonstrate precisely why the original concept of a single Blue Wave has ceased to describe Malaysian politics accurately.
The distinction is important.
The Blue Wave was originally associated with the extraordinary rise of Perikatan Nasional (PN), especially PAS, following GE15 and the subsequent state elections.
It conveyed the impression that Malay electoral sentiment was moving overwhelmingly and perhaps irreversibly towards PN.
But Malaysian politics has moved on.
PN itself has been thrown into institutional uncertainty.

The Registrar of Societies (RoS) suspended PN’s activities and issued the coalition a show-cause notice requiring it to explain why its registration should not be cancelled. Crucially, the RoS clarified that this was not yet an order of deregistration.
The legal distinction must be maintained. But its political implications should not be underestimated.

A coalition whose activities have been suspended while its very registration is being questioned cannot project the same organisational coherence that once allowed PN to portray itself as the principal vehicle of a national political wave.
More revealingly, the crisis emerged from tensions within PN itself. The problem was therefore not merely pressure imposed externally.
It reflected difficulties among the component parties that constituted the coalition.
PAS remains. Bersatu remains. Their respective grassroots networks and voters remain.
But the organisational umbrella connecting these forces has been seriously weakened.
This changes the meaning of Melaka.
Should BN win convincingly, the result should primarily be understood as a BN victory in Malacca — not automatically as another triumph of the Blue Wave.
BN’s blue is not PN’s blue. Their internal rivalries over lap deeply.
Umno has its own history, organisational machinery, political culture and grassroots structure.
PAS possesses another political tradition altogether. Bersatu has its own interests and calculations.
They can cooperate without becoming politically identical.
Indeed, the stronger BN becomes electorally, the more complicated their relationship becomes.
A weak BN has powerful reasons to cooperate with PN.
It needs additional votes, organisational support and ways of preventing damaging multi-cornered contests.
A resurgent BN faces a different calculation.
If Umno and BN can demonstrate through Johor, Negeri Sembilan and potentially Melaka that they remain capable of mobilising significant Malay support, their bargaining position changes substantially.
Why surrender constituencies that BN believes it can win itself ?
Indeed, why accept the assumption that PN should dominate conservative Malay politics ?
Moreover, why should an increasingly confident Umno subordinate its political future to another coalition ?
These are strategic questions that will become increasingly important approaching GE16. Malacca will all Umno and BN to look into these teasers.
In turn, the irony is therefore unmistakable. It will almost become a paradox to Malaysian politics.
The more convincingly BN wins Melaka, the more difficult it becomes to describe Malaysian politics as being driven by one amorphous Blue Wave.
There are now different shades of blue.
They overlap electorally, especially among Malay voters, but they are not interchangeable.
The Blue Wave thesis also risks obscuring another characteristic of contemporary Malaysian politics: extraordinary electoral fluidity.
Johor is not Negeri Sembilan.
Negeri Sembilan is not Melaka. Melaka will not automatically determine Selangor, Perak or GE16.
Malaysians have demonstrated repeatedly since 2018 that they are willing to change their political preferences.
State elections can turn on local leadership, candidate selection, machinery, turnout and state-specific concerns.
There are no political Nostradamuses in Malaysia.
Nor should Pakatan Harapan regard PN’s difficulties as an automatic political dividend.
The weakening of one opponent does not necessarily strengthen another.
Malay voters moving away from PN could migrate towards BN rather than PH. Equally, dissatisfied BN voters could move elsewhere.
The Unity Government must therefore continue confronting its own challenges of economic delivery, institutional reform, living costs and public confidence.
Neither should BN conclude that winning Melaka hands down guarantees victory at GE16.
Malaysia’s electoral landscape is becoming more multipolar, not less.
BN, PN’s constituent parties and PH possess different organisational strengths, geographical concentrations and demographic constituencies.
Sabah and Sarawak add another layer of complexity that makes any simplistic national-wave theory even more problematic.
What has therefore ended is not Malay political competition.
What has ended — or at least been seriously interrupted — is the assumption that this competition is moving inexorably in one direction under PN.
The suspension of PN’s activities and the possibility of deregistration have accelerated that change.
Even if PN eventually resolves its regulatory problems, the episode has exposed the fragility of coalition politics.
If BN now wins Melaka hands down, the message would be equally significant.
It would show that Umno and BN are capable of generating their own electoral momentum independent of PN.
Thus a BN landslide in Melaka would not necessarily be another manifestation of the Blue Wave.
It could be evidence of its fragmentation.
The political forces represented by PAS and Bersatu have not disappeared. Neither has Pakatan Harapan.
But the notion of one irresistible blue current sweeping across Peninsular Malaysia has become increasingly difficult to sustain.
Malaysia is entering something more complicated: competitive multipolar politics in which several political currents are struggling simultaneously for the same voters.
The Blue Wave may have been stopped.
The contest between the different shades of blue — and between them and Pakatan Harapan — is only intensifying. — Bernama
* Phar Kim Beng is professor of Asean Studies and director at the Institute of International and Asean Studies, International Islamic University Malaysia.

ccc9809cf20689db: NEW YORK, Oct 3 — An alleged gang rape at Cornell University, detailed in a graphic lawsuit last month, has provoked fury in the United States over sexual violence on campuses and colleges’ failure to stamp out the behavior.
The accuser has said that in 2024 she was drugged with ketamine, assaulted and raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, a social club for male students.
Her allegations fell within what activists call the “red zone,” a period at the start of the academic year when a large share of assaults happen, often at parties fueled by drugs and alcohol.

An estimated one in four female students and one in 14 male students experience rape or sexual assault at some point during their undergraduate studies, according to a 2020 study by the Association of American Universities.
Mental health nonprofit the Jed Foundation has reported that men in fraternities – which are routinely criticized for shielding sexism – are more likely to commit sexual violence.
The accused students in the Cornell case were members of the Chi Phi fraternity, one of several “Greek life” organizations common across US colleges.
Meanwhile, the accuser was part of a sorority for female students. Sorority members are statistically more likely than their non-affiliated peers to suffer sexual assault.
Consent
For Jennifer Freyd, a psychology professor at the University of Oregon, the Cornell case and the Ivy League college’s response are “so typical of other universities.”
Following the initial allegations in 2024, Cornell closed the fraternity and temporarily suspended the students allegedly involved, several of whom were later expelled.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The fraternity house at the centre of a rape allegation stands on the Cornell University campus on September 30, 2026. A former student, identified as Jane Doe, has alleged that she was drugged and raped by multiple men inside the Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024. — Getty Images pic via AFP
Meanwhile, the district attorney declined to prosecute because he said the victim’s police testimony did not establish a lack of consent.
The investigation was reopened after the complainant’s civil lawsuit fueled allegations that prosecutors and the elite college had failed to hold the men accountable.
Observers have noted that severe punishments like full expulsions are rare for fraternity members as they are often connected to elite networks and represent a key source of revenue for universities.
Freyd added that there should be a wider institutional approach of respecting whistleblowers when they come forward with accusations.
“That doesn’t mean they believe them without investigation, but it means that they take it seriously, and that they acknowledge the bravery involved,” she said.
Sex education
A further challenge in the Cornell case is a legal provision that makes it harder to prosecute rape cases in New York and several other US states if accusers were willingly intoxicated.
In response to growing public anger, New York Governor Kathy Hochul has vowed to work with lawmakers to close that loophole.
“Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” Hochul said.
The Democrat has also appointed Attorney General Letitia James, who has battled with President Donald Trump, as a special prosecutor for the Cornell case.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

New York Attorney General Letitia James (left) stands with Governor Kathy Hochul (right) at a news conference in Manhattan, where Hochul announced a review of Cornell University’s initial response to allegations that a former student was drugged and raped by multiple men at a campus fraternity in 2024. — Getty Images pic via AFP
Shiwali Patel, of the National Women’s Law Center, said she backed closing the legal loophole and added that better sex education is also crucial.
“One of the most effective ways of prevention is to have comprehensive sex education that is age developmentally appropriate from a young age, that includes talking about consent,” Patel said.
“But we are not seeing these changes being implemented, and so this issue is happening over and over again.” — AFP
511a311a51d208fc: BOGOTA, Oct 3 — China’s influence in Latin America is now viewed more positively than that of the United States, a major poll conducted in 17 Latin American countries showed yesterday.
The 2026 Latinobarometro survey showed that China overtaking the United States in terms of influence for the first time since the annual survey began in 1995.
It showed 57 per cent of people in Latin America considering the United States to be a positive influence, down from 60 per cent in 2020.
China, meanwhile, was considered a positive influence by 65 per cent of respondents, a jump from 48 per cent six years ago.
Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic were the only countries in the region where US influence was deemed more positive than that of China.
The report partly attributed the shift to Washington’s “almost complete absence” from the region in the two decades after the 2003 Iraq War.
During that time, Latin America “drew closer to other powers, to China, to the European Union, to Japan,” Marta Lagos, director of Latinobarometer, told AFP.
Lagos said China had won over Latin American populations by allowing them to access cheaper imports.
“The void that China fills is the void in people’s pockets, more than anything else,” she said.

The growing disaffection towards the United States comes nearly halfway through Trump’s second term, during which he has openly asserted his desire for hegemony over Latin America, as part of what he calls the “Donroe Doctrine.”
US popularity drops
As a country, the United States remains more popular than China, with 63 per cent saying they had a favourable view of the world’s top economy, compared to 58 per cent for its arch-rival.
But America’s popularity was markedly down compared to 2024, when Democratic president Joe Biden was in the White House and 73 per cent had a favourable view of the United States.

The “Donroe Doctrine” blends Trump’s first name with that of James Monroe, the fifth US president, who more than two centuries ago declared Latin America the United States’ exclusive sphere of influence.
Trump’s push to restore US dominance in what Washington calls “our hemisphere” was in evidence in January when the United States overthrew Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro.
The Latinobarometro poll showed a majority of people in all but one country — Argentina — approving of Maduro’s capture by US special forces.
But only 35 per cent considered it benefited Venezuela, compared to 28 per cent who said it harmed the Caribbean country.
Citizens of Venezuela itself were, however, among those who viewed US influence most positively.
Chile-based Latinobarometro is a non-profit organisation that surveys opinions on a range of issues, from democracy to the economy, security and migration.
The 2026 survey was based on some 19,200 face-to-face interviews carried out in 17 countries between May 7 and June 17, with a margin of error of 1 per cent. — AFP
a6327bf33f16b2e6: SOFIA, Oct 3 — More than a thousand years after his death, the remains of what may be Tsar Samuel, one of the last major rulers of the First Bulgarian Empire, are returning “home” on Saturday.
Greece and Bulgaria reached an agreement on their return this week, with Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev hailing the accord as “historic”.
Athens will in return receive 48 objects pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during World War I.
Samuel, who reigned from 997 to 1014, led several campaigns against the Byzantine Empire with his brothers, one of whom he later executed.
He gradually extended his authority over a swathe of the Balkans, making the Lake Prespa and Lake Ohrid region, now mostly in North Macedonia, his power base.
But the Byzantines regained the upper hand after 1001, soundly defeating Samuel’s army in 1014.
Samuel is said to have died of shock when he saw thousands of his defeated soldiers returning home blinded on the orders of Byzantine emperor Basil II, known as the “Bulgar Slayer”.
Samuel’s state fell under Byzantine rule four years later.
Bones of contention
But Bulgaria is not the only country to have claims on Samuel, with a huge statue of the tsar gracing the North Macedonian capital Skopje.
His legacy has become a bone of contention between the two neighbours, with Macedonians claiming him as “their” ruler.

The Skopje daily Sloboden Pechat called the handover another battle over history, with the Albanian-language daily Koha declaring: “The bones return, the conflict remains! Samuel once again (contested) between Skopje and Sofia.”
Some historians have likened the dispute to the French and German tug-of-war over Charlemagne.

In 2022, a bilateral commission recommended presenting Samuel as the head of a state that “most contemporary historiographers consider to be the Bulgarian Empire”, based in what is currently North Macedonia.
“Samuel occupies an important place in the historical narrative both in Bulgaria and in North Macedonia,” Dimitar Bechev, a researcher at the Carnegie Europe think tank, told AFP.
“This initiative aims to underline the Bulgarian character of the Slavic population of Macedonia,” he added.
The supposed remains of Samuel were discovered by Greek archaeologist Nikolaos Moutsopoulos in the 1960s.
Moutsopoulos led excavations on the Greek island of Saint Achilleios on Little Prespa Lake near the border between Greece and Albania and not far from the frontier with North Macedonia.
They found the skeleton of a man measuring about 1.6 metres (5 feet 3 inches), along with remnants of a rich silk fabric edged with gold and decorated with bird motifs.
The attribution to Samuel is based on clues including the location of the tomb, the sumptuousness of the garment, the age of the deceased and an old fracture.
Decades of negotiations
Bulgaria officially opened talks on the return of the remains in 2007, and they became a major issue in relations with Greece.
The deal this week also sparked a row in Bulgaria over who should claim the credit, with history playing a major role in this month’s presidential election.

Incumbent Iliana Iotova, backed by Radev and promoting ties both with Moscow and the EU and Nato, is playing the patriotic card, having launched her campaign in Veliki Preslav, former capital of the First Bulgarian Empire.
“Radev seeks to attract the patriotic electorate,” said analyst Bechev, with the message that unlike other nationalist parties, “he delivers results”.
Free trains are being laid on to the capital for the occasion, with some 750 police guarding the centre of Sofia during the handover ceremony.
The remains attributed to Samuel will be laid in a white sarcophagus made from marble quarried in the Prilep region of North Macedonia, public broadcaster BNT said.
They will rest in the Church of Saint Sofia, a sixth-century basilica that gave its name to the Bulgarian capital. — AFP
8fcc22714cff54b4: LOS ANGELES, Oct 3 — Sea levels in California are set to rise by as much as a foot (30 centimetres) in the coming days as an enormous wave washes up the US West Coast.

The huge surge of energy, known as a “coastal trapped wave” or a “Kelvin wave,” is part of El Nino, a months-long phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that scientists say could generate powerful storms and floods in some parts of the world, while leaving others in drought.

The Kelvin wave is not anything like a tsunami; nor does it crash on beaches. Rather it is a sustained bulge of excess water up to 30 kilometres wide that will hug the coastline as it travels all the way up to Alaska.
Dillon Amaya, an oceanographer at North Carolina State University, said the elevated sea levels could collide with other natural phenomena to create problems for coastal communities.

“What this wave is doing is it’s raising sea states, and then when... you combine this wave with things like storm surge from passing weather, large swells, or things like astronomically high tide... (you) elevate your risk for things like flooding and also beach erosion,” Amaya told AFP by telephone.
“The general rule of thumb is that every two to four inches (5-10 centimetres) of sea level rise that we see in that background state essentially doubles your flood risk.
“So it doesn’t sound like a lot, but because it’s over a huge volume of water, and it’s combined with these other factors, you start to get the flood risk.”
In recent weeks parts of Southern California have been hit by storm surges that have eaten away at beaches or damaged properties.
In Dana Point and Laguna Beach, south of Los Angeles, several houses have been left uninhabitable, and at least one has completely collapsed.
In Malibu, an enormous sink hole emerged in the driveway of a home belonging to Hollywood actor Nicolas Cage when pounding waves from a nearby hurricane eroded the coastline.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A person watches as a Pacific Ocean wave crashes into a seawall protecting beachfront homes on September 28, 2026 in Long Beach, California. Heavy surf generated by Hurricane Polo offshore, amid a Pacific Ocean heatwave and an emerging El Nino, led to a coastal flood advisory from the National Weather Service for much of Southern California. — Mario Tama/Getty Images North America/Getty Images pic via AFP
El Nino
The Kelvin wave is essentially both a cause and a symptom of El Nino, said Amaya, and originates in waters near Indonesia when trade winds die down.
“Those trade winds hold up a ton of really warm water in the Western Equatorial Pacific because they’re pushing on the surface waters as they blow.
“If they weaken for too long... water is then able to effectively slosh back along the equatorial strip from Indonesia all the way to South America.”
As this wave makes it way over the Pacific, it suppresses the cold water that usually comes up from the deep ocean, making the surface temperature higher.
It is this ocean warming that we call El Nino.
“So these Kelvin waves are, in many ways, the driving force of El Nino. They help El Nino grow and mature over the course of several months,” said Amaya.
As the equatorial Kelvin wave hits South America, the energy converts into a coastal Kelvin wave, and heads both north and south along the continents.

The wave going towards the US is currently somewhere north of Cabo, Mexico, and travelling around six miles (10 kilometres) an hour, said Amaya, who expects it to reach San Diego within the next week.
While Kelvin waves are common — there are five or six during every El Nino—this one arrives at a delicate time, said Amaya, with sea temperatures already elevated.
“When it gets really warm, that water expands... which causes sea levels to rise just because the water is warm, so you get an additional additive increase in sea level,” he said.

“Southern California... just got battered by offshore tropical cyclones, which led to flooding events already and beach erosion, so there’s lots of anxiety about extra flood risk coming from El Nino and these waves.” — AFP
04463804b7ce0a0d: OCTOBER 3 — Malaysia’s tourism industry is having a strong year. The country recorded 21.2 million international visitor arrivals in the first half of 2026 as Visit Malaysia 2026 brings renewed attention to the country’s tourism potential. The encouraging figures, however, also invite a broader question about what happens after visitors arrive. As the number of travellers grows, are we equally prepared for a new generation of visitors whose expectations of travel are changing?
The traveller is changing

Travel is no longer simply about visiting a destination and moving on to the next attraction. Increasingly, travellers want to understand and experience the places they visit, whether through local food, cultural activities, nature, community interaction or experiences that give them a stronger connection with the destination. Tourism Malaysia’s research found that exploring new experiences was the leading motivation among Malaysians planning international holidays, suggesting that the appeal of travel is increasingly tied to what people can experience rather than simply where they can go.

This shift matters because it changes the way destinations need to think about what they offer. A visitor may choose Malaysia because of its attractions, but the quality and uniqueness of the experience can influence whether that visitor stays longer, spends more locally or considers returning in the future.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Malaysia recorded 21.2 million international visitor arrivals in the first half of 2026 as Visit Malaysia 2026 brings renewed attention to the country’s tourism potential. — Picture by Yusof Mat Isa
Malaysia has more than places to offer

Malaysia is well positioned for this change because many of the experiences sought by travellers are already part of everyday life here. Our food, cultural traditions, heritage, natural landscapes and diverse communities provide opportunities that cannot easily be reproduced elsewhere, but these strengths need to be presented as experiences rather than simply listed as attractions.

A visitor who tastes a traditional dish, for example, can be offered more than a meal when the experience also introduces the story, people and traditions behind it. Likewise, a visit to a rural community can become more meaningful when travellers are given opportunities to understand local food, crafts, agriculture or customs rather than simply passing through the area.
The difference may seem small, but it can change how visitors remember a destination and how much value they attach to the overall trip.
A wider opportunity for local communities

This changing preference also creates opportunities beyond the conventional tourism industry. When travellers seek experiences, small businesses, local food operators, homestays, artisans, guides and community groups can all become part of the tourism offering, allowing tourism spending to reach people who may not benefit directly from large attractions or international hotel chains.

This is particularly relevant for smaller towns and rural areas, where the strength of tourism may lie not in major attractions but in local character. Encouraging visitors to eat locally, purchase locally made products, participate in community activities or spend more time in these areas can help spread the benefits of tourism beyond the usual destinations.
In this sense, the tourism boom can become an opportunity not only to attract visitors but also to create a wider economic role for local communities.
The experience does not end with the attraction

Creating memorable experiences, however, requires more than attractive destinations. The small details surrounding a trip can influence how visitors perceive Malaysia, from cleanliness and accessibility to hospitality, service quality and value for money. A destination may have everything needed to attract a visitor, but a poor experience along the way can affect whether that person recommends it or returns.

This means tourism businesses need to look beyond the product itself and consider the entire visitor experience. A meal, a homestay, a cultural activity or a nature excursion becomes more valuable when it is convenient, welcoming and meaningful to the visitor.
As expectations change, understanding the traveller becomes just as important as promoting the destination.
Are we ready?

Malaysia does not need to create a completely new tourism identity because much of what today’s travellers are looking for is already here. What matters now is how well we connect these strengths and turn them into experiences that visitors can discover, enjoy and remember.

Visit Malaysia 2026 provides an opportunity to do exactly that, but the success of the tourism boom should not be judged only by the number of people arriving at our borders. It should also be reflected in the quality of their experiences, the opportunities created for local businesses and communities, and the reasons they have to return.

Malaysia has plenty of places worth visiting. The next challenge is to make those places worth experiencing, while ensuring that the people who make those experiences possible are part of the growth that follows.

* Dr Nurul Fardini Zakaria is a Senior Lecturer in Marketing at the School of Business Management, Universiti Utara Malaysia (UUM), with expertise in consumer behaviour, digital marketing, sustainable consumption and consumer welfare.

9d75799e618dd345: MELAKA, Oct 3 — The physical and mental well-being of senior citizens will be among the key areas addressed under the Senior Citizens Bill, which is expected to be tabled in the Cabinet soon, said Women, Family and Community Development Minister Datuk Seri Nancy Shukri.

Nancy said the bill reflected the government’s commitment to strengthening support, protection and care systems for senior citizens, ensuring they remain relevant to current needs and future demographic changes in the country.

Commenting on the issue of independent speakers, Nancy said her ministry was ready to cooperate with relevant parties to screen individuals appointed to deliver talks to ensure they had the necessary qualifications and calibre.

56d246e785ffc84e: SEPANG, Oct 3 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim today attended the Formula One (F1) Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix qualifying session at the Sepang International Circuit (SIC), where he also inspected preparations and the overall running of the race.

97a54f6c4eaf2b77: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 3 — Malaysia’s economic focus has shifted from pursuing efficiency to building greater resilience as the country continues to outperform growth forecasts despite global uncertainty, the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) said.

89f7165e2ebfe859: "Can it run Doom?" now applies to databases, as the author of DOOMQL has released a far more visually accurate port. There's a saying: "Be careful what you wish for." In 2025, we wrote a piece about a database boffin coming up with a version of Doom that was written in SQL. It was neat, but the visuals were nearer to 3D Monster Maze than to the 90s pixel blaster. We commented, "If persuading SQL to do the entire rendering pipeline is a 'bad idea,' we cannot wait for a terrible one." And so here we are. The author, Lukas Vogel, has been at it again and ported both Doom's game logic and renderer to SQL, running it in a database. Python handles timing, keyboard input, and bitmap display, but the rest comes from SQL queries and the CedarDB database. DOOMQL was an undeniably impressive thing. However, Vogel told The Register, "Someone on Hacker News complained last year when I did the first iteration that that one was more Wolfenstein-like because I used raycasting instead of BSP-tree traversal which was *the thing* that made Doom revolutionary. "So I obviously couldn't let that stand." Which brings us to SQLDoom. Doom, ported to SQL. In his blog, Vogel noted the ground rules for the port. Unlike DOOMQL, this had to look like real Doom. The rendering had to be purely SQL-based: "the only acceptable SQL output is a table or a bitmap encoding exact RGB values for every pixel," and the game loop also had to be purely SQL-based. Vogel told us, "I was very thrilled to find out that porting the real Doom was a) feasible and b) the performance was actually *better* than the much more barebones approach from last year! "Also, at some point I started actually playing it for fun in my free time, which is still a very strange feeling. I intended it as a tech demo, but it just feels like the real Doom, even though it doesn't share a single line of code with any existing Doom port. So I wanted to see how far I could take it. "In the end, I even got deathmatch to work." According to Vogel, the game is perfectly playable on his laptop (using a Ryzen 7 7840U), and multiplayer games can be played online using EU and US servers. We found the server performance a little sluggish – likely more due to the servers than the port – although getting SQL to jump through these hoops is something that, only a few short years ago, would be unimaginable. It's worth keeping in mind that this is a thinly veiled demonstration of the capabilities of CedarDB. It's a compiling database system where complex queries are eventually compiled to machine code. Still, it's hard not to get swept up in Vogel's enthusiasm and the fact that this is Doom… running in a database. Certainly this is a lot more fun than recreating yet another online store for yet another interminable keynote. ®
38c2c2ff8ab56a47: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 3 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has urged Malaysia’s youth to master emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing to drive economic growth.

“Digital transformation requires AI. Otherwise, we will fall behind in development and in our ability to strengthen the economy.

Anwar said while digital transformation and high-technology economic development were essential, such progress should not come at the expense of ethics, morality and human values.

Anwar said the government would continue to improve the quality of education, strengthen proficiency in Bahasa Melayu and English, and give young Malaysians opportunities to master other languages, including Chinese, Tamil, Arabic, French and German.

“I am confident that if this is the new spirit, we will see our country move forward at speed and, within 10 years, we will no longer recognise the Malaysia of today. Instead, we will see a new, vibrant, progressive and successful Malaysia,” he said. — Bernama

46ebd6a040f3783a: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 3 — Datuk Seri Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man said most PAS leaders could not attend Tun Dr Hasmah Mohd Ali’s funeral because they had prior commitments at home and abroad.
The party’s deputy president said PAS had conveyed its condolences directly to former prime minister Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad and his family, according to Sinar Harian.

2a405404d7b8a714: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 3 — Malaysian youths today have three main concerns, including whether their existing jobs would still exist in the next decade, Youth and Sports Minister Dr Mohammed Taufiq Johari said today.

Speaking at the Perdana Fellows Alumni Association’s (PFAA) Youth Economic Forum 2026 (YEF 2026), Dr Taufiq said his ministry had been part of a Budget roadshow in six zones nationwide to engage with youths ahead of the government’s upcoming Budget 2027.
He noted that the youths did not ask theoretical questions, and summarised their questions as revolving around three main concerns.
“Firstly, can youths bear the cost of living?

“Secondly, will my job today still exist 10 years from now? And the third question that is frequently mentioned by youths, if I fall, who will help me?” he said ahead of the tabling of the government’s Budget 2027 in Parliament next Friday.

Dr Taufiq said the panel discussions at today’s YEF on artificial intelligence, talent, green energy and social protection would answer these questions, as youths would not feel the benefits of government policies if those policies fail to address their anxieties.
While saying that youths are often told to be strong and to upskill themselves, Dr Taufiq said that being strong or resilient is not a policy.

“Being strong is what the public is forced to do temporarily while they wait for policies to come. Our duty is to create a protection system that is strong enough so that Malaysia’s youths do not have to ‘bersusah payah’ (toil) to be heroes just to continue living,” he said.

He added that the federal government is currently working on raising both the ceiling and the floor of the economy to ensure that all citizens feel the benefits from foreign direct investments into Malaysia.
He thanked the youths for their proposals on developing the country, and expressed hope that they could also help build the nation together.

At the YEF 2026, which carried the theme of “Decoding the Next Decade: Advancing Malaysia’s Economic Frontier”, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim received six policy proposals that the PFAA had developed based on a nationwide survey of more than 2,000 youths.

The six proposals covered artificial intelligence (AI), green entrepreneurship, skills development, better public services, foreign direct investment, and establishing a National Youth Economic Action Council to give youths a permanent platform to make economic policies.
Anwar also received a memorandum on the youths’ proposals for Budget 2027 at the forum.
Anwar hints at Budget 2027 help for hungry university students, urges youth to lead now
8bccf837209a09f6: LONDON, Oct 3 — A UK-Iranian dual national arrested over a mysterious incident near a British military airbase has been released on bail, counter-terrorism police said on Saturday.
The 25-year-old was arrested in central London on Thursday “on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts” as part of an investigation into events near RAF Fairford in southwest England on Sunday.
Five other men arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences near the airbase in Gloucestershire were also released on bail earlier this week.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, a claim Tehran has rejected.
But the source and nature of the threat near the airbase – used by the US military in its war against Iran – have remained shrouded in mystery.

Police were called to the base early on Sunday after reports that “suspicious” white vans were heading towards it, triggering the evacuation of a nearby village and the declaration of a “major incident”.
Days later, police said no explosives had been found at the scene.
Adding to the mystery, British media reported that officers were alerted to the incident by one of the initial suspects, although police have not commented on the reports.
Washington has further muddied the waters by criticising the release of the suspects on bail and declaring hostile state involvement early in the investigation.
“The investigation into the circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is continuing,” UK police said in an update on Saturday. — AFP
fd447d5ccac23652: This year, members of Seattle Mountain Rescue have been setting off into the wilds of the US Pacific Northwest wearing an unusual piece of kit.

Devices like these are called human exoskeletons. They attach to parts of the body to create an external—or “exo”—mechanical structure. This powered frame enhances the wearer’s physical capabilities.
028b039dcf0ebfb6: HANOI, Oct 3 — Vietnam’s quarterly growth surged to 9.95 per cent in the July-September period, up from 8.81 per cent in the previous three months and the fastest pace in four years, according to government data.
The country has long been a success story among Asian economies, with its communist government targeting double-digit expansion over the next five years.
Growth for the first nine months of 2026 came in at 9.01 per cent, the fastest for the period in 15 years, the National Statistics Office said.
Exports rose 24.5 per cent year on year, while imports increased 36.7 per cent.
Vietnam notched 8 per cent annual growth last year, among the highest in the world despite new tariffs imposed by its largest export market, the United States.
The Asian Development Bank late last month revised up its forecast for Vietnam’s 2026 annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth to 7.8 per cent, from 7.2 per cent forecast in July.
The upgrade was “underpinned by continued expansion in manufacturing, buoyant domestic consumption, and sustained foreign direct investment”, it said.
But it warned that weaker global demand and geopolitical uncertainty could weigh on growth.
In September, FTSE Russell upgraded Vietnam’s stock market to secondary emerging market status. — AFP
a2b6ea0cca86f4e3: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 3 — Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim today said he, as the prime minister, would not allow anyone to embezzle or steal money, recalling a lesson from his own childhood as he continued his firm stance against corruption in Malaysia.

Anwar today described a lesson he had learnt from his grandmother when he was a primary school student aged around eight or nine, after he took nutmegs from a small farm on a hill in Bukit Mertajam, Penang.
Anwar described his grandmother’s questioning, where he confirmed he did not buy and also did not get permission to take those nutmegs from a farm.

“But I said ‘Chinese farm’. So I thought Chinese farm, Malay steal, it’s ok. I was aged eight or nine,” he said in his speech at the Youth Economic Forum (YEF) 2026 at the Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre.
“My grandmother said ‘No, if they are taken without permission, from whoever it is, even if they were four nutmegs, it is theft. And stealing is a sin,” he said.
Anwar said he had then decided to not eat the nutmegs and to return them the next day, but said his grandmother had insisted that he return them the same day itself.
Recalling that it was nearly 7pm and with all his friends having already returned home, Anwar said he then ran uphill in the dark and that he had felt afraid when he heard the sound of dogs.

“I took the four nutmegs and threw them back to that area. I ran back and cried, because I did not understand why my grandmother was so firm in ensuring discipline, because I stole four nutmegs and I can return them tomorrow.
“But that taught me, when (I) become prime minister, don’t steal and don’t allow others to steal,” he said to loud claps from the youth gathered at the plenary hall in KLCC.
He said he hoped youths would understand why it is important to master knowledge and also know what is considered wrong, and also urged them to maintain their values.

Before sharing his childhood story, Anwar had alluded to those who are corrupt when saying that Malaysia is not poor, but that the country had lost billions of its riches due to the practices of “penyakau” (thieves).
He urged youths in Malaysia to rise up to reject corruption, urging them not to compromise against “penyakau”.
Countering those who might accuse him of highlighting politics to youths, Anwar said youths may not be vocal, but are aware that theft is wrong.

He pointed out that even stealing a pencil or pen in school would result in reprimand from teachers, and questioned how stealing billions of ringgit when one has grown up to be a leader would be morally or ethically acceptable.
Earlier in his speech, Anwar emphasised the importance of morals and criticised those who may consider corruption acceptable as it involves their own race.

“There are people who told me, ‘This Datuk Anwar highlights corruption issues — 1MDB, Tabung Haji, Felda. These are Malay bodies. Don’t criticise, these are Malay bodies’. So if it’s Malay bodies, can ‘songlap’, ‘sakau’? Where did you learn this from? This is a damaged way of thinking,” he said.

The words “songlap” and “sakau” are generally used to refer to theft, with Anwar saying that Malaysia has the capability to rise further but that billions had been lost through 1Malaysia Development Berhad, Lembaga Tabung Haji and Felda.

Anwar said he was highlighting all these to the youth as he believes they still have idealism and want the country to be dignified, also believing that they “hate misappropriation, corruption and leaders who use their powers to gain riches”.

“Because the youths know many are still good, will uplift those who are good and reject those who are clearly corrupt and abused their powers,” Anwar said to loud cheers and claps from the youths gathered here.

ea7b3253b6b73845: SEPANG, Oct 3 — Four-time world champion Max Verstappen continued his dominant form for Red Bull by claiming his first pole of the season on Saturday after topping qualifying for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The 29-year-old Dutchman, currently sixth in the world championship standings, clocked a best lap of 1min 35.130sec in the final minute of a close session held in high temperatures at the Sepang International Circuit.

“It’s fantastic,” said a delighted Verstappen.
“We’ve been trying for many Grands Prix to get a pole position and so to finally get it is pretty incredible.
“I’m happy with today and will try to win tomorrow.”

880287db23c6335e: BATU PAHAT, Oct 3 — The daughter of a couple who died in a road crash at Kilometre 72.5 of Jalan Batu Pahat-Mersing yesterday never expected an incident she initially thought was minor to claim her parents’ lives.

“At first, I thought it was just a minor accident... my husband tried calling my sister’s mobile phone, but someone else answered and said our parents had been pronounced dead at the scene. The person who answered was a driver right behind their car.

“Over the past week, my late father kept cleaning the compound thoroughly, sweeping the grounds, mowing the lawn, and doing other chores as if he knew many people would come over,” she said.

Fire and Rescue Department personnel at the scene of a fatal crash involving a Hyundai Matrix car and a lorry at Kilometre 72.5 of Jalan Batu Pahat-Mersing in Kluang, Johor on October 2, 2026. — Picture from Facebook/This is Johor

5014b38aa281e81d: “I always laugh at the IT industry’s terms,” says Ryan Sheehan, a senior vice president at $16 billion global solutions integrator SHI. And right now the jargon that gets him giggling is “forward-deployed engineer” (FDE) because, as he told The Register at VMware's September Explore conference, “We have been doing FDE for a long time.” “Doing FDE” involves sending top consultants to a client, without tying them to a project. Instead they get a mission to build something valuable using new technology, and carte blanche to make that happen in a hurry. Sheehan has company in believing FDEs aren’t fundamentally new. Cloud monitoring vendor DoIT told The Register it has used FDEs since 2011, but only started using the term in the last quarter of 2025, when it changed the name of its “Customer Reliability Engineering” practice to FDE. That decision came as services companies adopted the term FDE to describe the work needed to build AI proofs of concept. The name has its origins at Palantir, whose chief technology officer Shyam Sankar claims he coined it in 2007 after a conversation in which his CEO Alex Karp asked him why French restaurants are so good. Karp apparently answered his own question by saying, “The wait staff is actually part of the kitchen staff. They intimately understand the food, the methodology, and the technique. They are not merely carrying the food from the kitchen to the table, but are instead part of a subtle and complex system that affects kitchen operations.” Sankar says Karp asked him “to build that, but for engineering” so he did and called it “forward deployed engineering.” “FDEs embed alongside our customers and work to ensure our software solves their problem and not some proxy for their problem,” Sankar wrote on his personal Substack. “They’re crazy enough to get on a last-minute plane to Iraq, they’re smart enough to ship quality, same-day code, and their EQ is still high enough to talk to users (and maybe even enjoy it).” Sankar says Palantir’s investors thought FDEs were a bad idea because the costs they incurred ate into margins, but says they’re worth it because they ensure customers understand the company’s products and how to get value from them. “We didn’t believe in throwing our software over the wall in the hopes the customer would divine the correct meaning from it,” Shankar wrote. “This approach built an engineering organization with unmatched creativity, responsiveness, and focus on the primacy of winning.” AWS likes winning, too, and in June announced a dedicated AWS FDE organization, and $1 billion to fund it. In July Microsoft trumped that with a $2.5 billion so-called “Frontier Company” it claims “goes beyond” FDEs. Both companies see FDEs as a way to get their consultants into customers to help them build AI apps. They argue FDEs’ time has come because, as Palantir found when users struggled to put its software to work, organizations often struggle to turn AI experiments into production applications. Stop us if you've heard this one before But vendors also admit that FDEs aren’t entirely new. Indeed, AWS told The Register it has offered customers something very similar to an FDE for years. “We started this journey all the way back in 2017 when the focus was machine learning (ML),” said Taimur Rashid, the cloud giant’s managing director for go to market, Frontier AI Engineering & Services. “We created a team called the ML Solutions Lab. The idea was that the tech is new, customers need to navigate it. So we said ‘Why don’t we loan them a data scientist?’ They can build a PoC, and the customer can build on our platform.” Rashid says AWS sometimes called this sort of arrangement a “secondment,” a “resident architect” or a “resident scientist.” Whatever you call it, Rashid said the approach worked well so AWS decided to evolve it when generative AI burst onto the scene – this time using an applied scientist and a strategist, and an evolved approach. “We forward-deploy them – they will help to identify the art of the possible and develop the solution for you or with you,” Rashid explained. “They will be part of your business and operational workflows, and effectively be yours for a defined time,” he said. That’s different to conventional services engagements, he argues, because there’s no scope of work, no hourly charge for consultants’ services. “What is different about FDE is you are saying the customer wants to build. The path is not determined.” Carlos Pereira, a Fellow and Chief Architect in Cisco’s Customer Experience team, also admited FDEs aren’t entirely new, but argued AI makes them more valuable than conventional consultants. "The idea of an expert being embedded on-site to help a customer adopt new technology and solutions isn't new,” he told The Register by email. “Our Customer Success organization has been doing this for years.” “The evolution is that AI is now a key part of that equation,” he added. “It introduces new variables like non-deterministic AI models, evaluations, faster-moving requirements, and specialized skills that not every customer team has in-house.” Analyst firms Gartner and Forrester agree that FDEs can be useful, and that this form of IT services differs due to greater intimacy between client and consultant. “They often have full-stack access to the customer’s environment and the vendor’s codebase, allowing them to build and iterate in real time,” Gartner’s Arun Chandrasekaran and Robert Thanaraj wrote in March guidance titled “An AI Leader’s Guide to Forward Deployed Engineering to Scale AI.” A June best practice report from five Forrester analysts, titled “Forward-Deployed Engineers: Use provider-embedded builders to improve outcomes,” praises the model for helping to “accelerate adoption and turn complex platforms into production-ready outcomes.” Yet both analyst firms also warn that using FDEs may see clients develop a dependency on the vendor that provides them. “The allure of delivering outcomes at speed can induce blind spots and is fraught with risks,” according to Forrester. “Without the appropriate guardrails on tech architecture and stack choices, teams can fall into a bespoke trap, where highly tailored solutions deepen vendor dependence and make future change costly.” Debt and dependency Gartner urges would-be hirers of FDEs to “beware of ill-conceived FDE engagements that can lead to a high degree of vendor dependency, security/data risk exposure, technical debt, and talent atrophy.” The latter happens when organizations hire FDEs but don’t train their own teams on new tech. “Your internal team may become operators of a black box rather than architects, making it difficult to innovate without the vendor,” Gartner warns. Gartner also worries FDEs can be a fast-track to technical debt. “A major concern with the FDE model is that it relies heavily on manually designed structures and hard-coded domain knowledge. Such human-engineered components tend to deliver short-term gains but are repeatedly superseded as more general, scalable learning systems improve.” “As large language models continue to advance, much of this manually encoded logic is likely to be rendered obsolete, requiring costly rework or full redesign, and creating a long-term technical and organizational burden.” FDEs themselves may soon be obsolete, because they’re not vendors’ only bet on improving AI consultancy skills, according to Omdia chief analyst Jay McBain. “At the same time as investing in FDEs, the big players have been investing big into partner enablement,” he told The Register. “They are playing both ends.” The tech services channel doesn’t mind that, because according to Omdia data 82 percent of partners report they “aren’t ready” to quickly grow their AI services. The vendors promoting FDEs, meanwhile, don’t want to use this form of consultancy for long. “None of these companies’ investors want to dilute a low-value services business into the overall revenue,” McBain wrote. “We are predicting all of this FDE investment will fall back into the channel by 2031 when this matures.” Which rather suggests that in a few years we’ll all be laughing at how Palantir re-heated an old form of tech services under a new name, and the rest of the industry decided to follow the same recipe. ®

c6df0ba4697c2ff2: Pearly Tan-M Thinaah did their job.
They fought their way into the Asian Games semi-finals, pushed the world No 1 Chinese pair hard and brought home Malaysia’s only badminton medal from Aichi-Nagoya.
It was a bronze, and Malaysia’s first women’s doubles medal at the Games in 12 years. Pearly and Thinaah deserve every bit of credit.
But one pair on the podium cannot disguise what happened around them.

Malaysia’s men’s singles players were gone by the last 16. Aaron Chia-Tee Kai Wun fell in the same round, while Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin Rumsani went out in the quarter-finals. Neither mixed doubles combination reached the last eight.
For a badminton nation with Malaysia’s resources, depth and expectations, this should prompt more than another round of post-tournament analysis.
Has Malaysian badminton become jaded? And, somewhere amid the reshuffles, reviews and long-term plans, has the Badminton Association of Malaysia (BAM) lost the plot?
The problem is not a lack of talent. Malaysia has players capable of beating the best. The frustration is how often that potential appears in flashes without becoming sustained performance.
The men’s doubles situation offers a telling example.
Aaron Chia and Soh Wooi Yik were split, with Aaron paired with Tee Kai Wun. BAM has presented the changes as part of its longer-term planning towards the 2028 Olympics.
That is a legitimate objective but long-term planning cannot become a convenient shelter for every short-term disappointment.
Experiments must produce evidence. New pairings need a clear purpose, and players must know what they are building towards. Otherwise, movement starts to look like direction.
Razif Sidek, one of Malaysia’s great doubles players, has warned about the risks of major changes before a big tournament.
He felt the reshuffling affected seeding and exposed Malaysia to difficult opponents early. He also backed Aaron and Tee, while acknowledging that they remain some distance behind the leading pairs.
The issue is not whether BAM should experiment. It should. The issue is whether it knows when an experiment has yielded enough information to stop.
The national and independent systems cannot be treated as separate planets. Players move between them. Some train outside BAM but still represent Malaysia; others return to the national setup.
That fluidity can be an asset, provided the pathway makes sense. BAM should be able to explain how talent is identified, developed, paired, tested and promoted, regardless of where a player trains.
Too much of the conversation, however, revolves around the latest combination rather than the larger plan.
Then there is Nova Widianto.

The Indonesian left BAM at the end of July after more than three years in charge of the mixed doubles programme. His most significant achievement was guiding Chen Tang Jie and Toh Ee Wei to Malaysia’s first mixed doubles world title in 2025.
BAM thanked him for his contribution but did not disclose why he left. By early September, it had yet to finalise his replacement.
At Aichi-Nagoya, Tang Jie partnered Cheng Su Yin, while Goh Soon Huat and Shevon Lai formed Malaysia’s other mixed doubles combination. Neither reached the quarter-finals.
There is no evidence that Nova’s departure caused those results. It would be simplistic to claim otherwise but the timing deserves scrutiny.
Back with Indonesia, Nova guided Amri Syahnawi and Nita Violina Marwah to the Asian Games final, where they won silver.

That does not prove BAM made the wrong decision in allowing him to leave. It does raise a more pertinent question: did the association have a succession plan before one of its most successful recent coaches departed?
The questions extend beyond the coaching bench. They reach the leadership itself.

BAM president Tengku Zafrul Aziz has put forward Tangkis 2030 as a roadmap for Malaysian badminton and appointed Lee Chong Wei to chair the Performance Committee. Zafrul has chosen not to chair a committee himself, citing the need to avoid conflicts of interest.
That is a matter of structure, not an escape from responsibility.

A president need not dictate coaching tactics or choose a doubles partner. But he must ensure that the people entrusted with those decisions are working towards clear targets, that their performance is reviewed and that shortcomings lead to action.
What does Zafrul regard as measurable progress under Tangkis 2030? When does he decide that a strategy is not working? And who must answer when it fails to deliver?
Lee’s stature in Malaysian badminton is beyond argument. His record as a player makes him one of the sport’s defining figures in this country.
But being a great player and managing high-performance sport are different jobs.

Lee has chaired BAM’s Performance Committee since October 2025. The committee works with the coaching and player-development structure on performance. That makes its work a legitimate subject for examination.

After nearly a year, what has actually changed under Lee’s chairmanship? What evidence supports the decisions to alter pairings? How does the committee measure progress, and what happens when targets are missed?
These are questions about Lee the administrator, not Lee the legend.
The same scrutiny must apply to the singles programme.
Kenneth Jonassen took charge of the men’s singles only in January 2025. It would be unfair to lay a decade of disappointment at the feet of a coach who has been in the job for less than two years.
But Malaysia cannot keep talking about the future without defining when it is expected to arrive.
Both singles programmes need a serious review of tactics, consistency, preparation and player development. Not another promise that the next generation will come good.
China is no longer the only benchmark
The wider Asian badminton landscape is changing. China remains formidable, but it no longer sets the entire rhythm of the sport.
Indonesia, Korea, Japan, India, Thailand and others have developed players and combinations capable of challenging the established order.
That should create opportunities for Malaysia. Instead, it makes the lack of clarity harder to excuse.
If the gap at the top is narrowing, BAM should be identifying where Malaysia can close it. It cannot do so by endlessly rearranging the furniture.
Aichi-Nagoya must be treated as more than a medal tally.

Malaysia has the talent, experience and institutional knowledge to expect more. What it needs is a clear connection between them, backed by decisions that can be measured and leaders prepared to answer for the results.
The danger is not one unsatisfactory tournament. It is becoming too accustomed to explaining why the next one will be different.
At some point, explanations become a substitute for progress, and Malaysian badminton cannot afford to mistake the two.

3accee4374e9bdc8: From P Sundramoorthy

The current debate over house arrest has opened an important conversation about the future of Malaysia’s criminal justice system. The immediate issue concerns the legal basis, eligibility, safeguards and judicial oversight of house arrest.

But from a criminological perspective, the bigger question is whether Malaysia has a sufficiently integrated mechanism to continuously examine emerging challenges across policing, prosecution, courts, corrections, rehabilitation and crime prevention.

Malaysia does not currently have a dedicated statutory framework comprehensively governing house arrest. Recent reporting has highlighted questions concerning the legal basis, implementation, monitoring, restrictions and accountability surrounding such arrangements.

A constitutional lawyer has described the situation as entering relatively “uncharted” legal territory, while a December 2025 High Court decision raised questions about whether an existing legal provision could be used to implement house arrest in the absence of specific legislation.

This does not mean that house arrest itself is necessarily inappropriate. Modern correctional systems in several jurisdictions use forms of home detention, parole, electronic monitoring and supervised community release.

Malaysia itself has operated a parole system since 2008, with the Parole Board required to consider matters including public safety, the nature of the offence, criminal history, risk of reoffending, reintegration and the impact on victims.
The lesson is that alternatives to imprisonment require clear legislation, transparent criteria, professional risk assessment, supervision and accountability.
The central criminological concern, therefore, should be system design rather than personalities.

Any future house-arrest legislation should clearly establish eligibility, exclusions, risk assessment, electronic monitoring, breach procedures, judicial oversight, victims’ interests, review mechanisms and reporting requirements. It should also clearly distinguish between administrative discretion, correctional management, judicial sentencing and constitutional clemency.
Without such clarity, different institutions may interpret their respective powers differently, creating uncertainty and potentially undermining public confidence.
However, house arrest is only one example of a much larger problem. Malaysia's criminal justice system is confronting increasingly complex challenges.

Organised crime is becoming more transnational; cybercrime and technology-enabled fraud are expanding; artificial intelligence is creating new opportunities for both criminals and law enforcement; drug trafficking networks continue to evolve; financial crime increasingly exploits social engineering; youth offending presents changing patterns; and prisons face continuing challenges involving overcrowding, rehabilitation, illicit activity and reintegration.

These problems cannot be examined exclusively through the perspective of one institution. A police response alone cannot solve organised crime. Prison expansion alone cannot solve recidivism. Longer sentences alone cannot necessarily reduce offending. Public awareness alone cannot adequately address sophisticated financial scams.
Likewise, new laws introduced in response to individual controversies may create unintended consequences if their wider criminological and operational implications are not assessed beforehand.
This is why I have, on several occasions, proposed the establishment of a Criminal Justice Advisory Commission for Malaysia.

Such a commission should not replace the courts, Parliament, the police, the Attorney-General's Chambers, the prisons department or existing oversight bodies. Rather, it should provide an independent, multidisciplinary and evidence-based mechanism to examine the criminal justice system across institutional boundaries.

Its mandate could include reviewing crime trends, policing strategies, prosecution and case-management issues, sentencing policy, prison population and overcrowding, parole and community corrections, rehabilitation, recidivism, victim protection, juvenile offending, organised and transnational crime, cybercrime, corruption risks and emerging technologies.
It should also examine whether laws introduced for one purpose are producing unintended consequences elsewhere in the system.
International examples of system-wide coordination

England and Wales have a Criminal Justice Board bringing together senior leaders from policing, prosecution, courts, prisons, probation and other justice institutions to maintain oversight and promote collaboration.

New Zealand has a Justice Sector Leadership Board providing shared direction across six core justice agencies, supported by a dedicated directorate for system-wide coordination. New Zealand has also used independent advisory groups to facilitate wider public discussion and evidence-based criminal justice reform.
Proposed model
Malaysia should consider a model appropriate to its own constitutional and institutional circumstances.

The proposed commission should ideally comprise criminologists, scholars, former and serving practitioners, legal experts, corrections specialists, psychologists, victim representatives, data and technology experts and civil society representatives. Its membership should be professionally credible and sufficiently independent to provide frank advice, including advice that may be inconvenient to government or individual institutions.

Importantly, the commission should be evidence-driven rather than politically driven. It should have access, subject to appropriate confidentiality and privacy safeguards, to reliable data from the police, prosecution service, courts and corrections system.

Malaysia needs better integration of criminal justice data so that policymakers can see the entire journey from reported crime and investigation through prosecution, conviction, sentencing, imprisonment, parole, rehabilitation and reoffending.

For example, instead of asking only how many crimes are reported, policymakers should also examine detection rates, charging decisions, conviction outcomes, sentence patterns, prison admissions, time served, parole outcomes and recidivism. Such information would enable criminal justice policy to be evaluated according to measurable outcomes rather than public perception alone.
Reporting

The commission should publish regular reports to Parliament, perhaps at least twice a year, identifying emerging risks, evaluating existing policies and proposing reforms. The government should be required to respond formally to major recommendations, while retaining the constitutional and democratic authority to accept, modify or reject them.

This would complement, rather than duplicate, existing oversight mechanisms. Malaysia already has institutions such as the Independent Police Conduct Commission, whose statutory functions include investigating police misconduct and reporting annually to Parliament. The proposed commission would operate at a different level: looking principally at the criminal justice system as an interconnected whole.
A modern criminal justice system cannot afford to operate primarily in reaction to crises. It needs foresight, reliable data, independent expertise and continuous evaluation.
Malaysia has invested considerably in policing, prosecution, courts and corrections. The next step should be to strengthen the connective tissue between them.

A Criminal Justice Advisory Commission would provide one possible institutional mechanism for doing precisely that, helping Malaysia move from reactive criminal justice policymaking towards a more coordinated, evidence-based and forward-looking system of justice, public safety and rehabilitation.
P Sundramoorthy is a criminologist at the Centre for Policy Research at Universiti Sains Malaysia and an FMT reader.

3442c9fdac4b6ecf: Yang Dipertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir’s recent dismissal of the entire executive council has left Negeri Sembilan in limbo.
Menteri besar Ismail Lasim has been left to run the administration alone, relying on civil servants to keep the machinery of government moving.
At the Aug 1 state election, Barisan Nasional won 18 of the 36 state assembly seats on offer, one short of an outright simple majority—and was only propped up by support from PAS.

Initially, Jalaluddin Alias—the man who led Umno’s withdrawal of support for the previous administration—was tipped to take over as MB. However, it was Ismail who was sworn in, with Jalaluddin overlooked even for a seat on the 10-man exco lineup.
Ismail himself has been mired in controversy.

Soon after pledging his allegiance to Tuanku Muhriz, he signed a proclamation seeking the ruler’s removal, then disavowed it on grounds of coercion, before affirming it again—this time unanimously with the rest of his exco.
That last act was enough for the entire exco to be sacked on grounds of disloyalty to the ruler, leaving Ismail the last man standing.
Ismail may have survived the cull, but was his own conduct proper? Does he still have the moral authority to remain menteri besar?
Even if he clings to office, Ismail cannot form a functioning exco. His entire 10-man team has already betrayed the ruler and been sacked. Surely, they cannot be reappointed.
With Jalaluddin presumably not in contention, Ismail is left to choose from the assemblymen he originally bypassed. But do Negeri Sembilan voters deserve a government of second-choice leaders?
Previous legitimacy crises
Malaysia has faced constitutional turmoil before.

In 1977, Kelantan plunged into crisis when PAS clashed with Umno, prompting an emergency and suspension of the state assembly. In 2009, Perak’s defections sparked a bitter legal battle over who commanded the confidence of the house.
In both cases, governance collapsed when legitimacy was in doubt.

So what of Negeri Sembilan today? Who will debate land policies, laws, and budgets? Who will table motions, approve bills, and scrutinize expenditure? Who will raise constituency issues on behalf of voters?
Time to face the truth
The reality is stark. BN, despite its numbers, has no clear path to government and stability. In any case, Negeri Sembilan’s people deserve better.
The time for political games is over.
Either dissolve the assembly and return the mandate to the people, or accept that only a unity government can salvage what remains of Negeri Sembilan’s dignity.
Anything less would be a betrayal of the state and its citizens.
